points: Germany's invasion of France followed the Schlieffen Plan, but the advance was checked at the First Battle of the Marne, fought from 5 to 12 September 1914.
After the Marne both sides moved northwards in the race to the sea, which ended with a continuous line of trenches from the North Sea to the Swiss border by late 1914.
On the Eastern Front, German forces under Hindenburg and Ludendorff defeated Russian armies at Tannenberg from 26 to 30 August 1914.
Britain's small professional army, the British Expeditionary Force, was largely destroyed in the first months of fighting, and it was rebuilt through volunteer recruitment.

notes.h: Trench warfare and the Western Front
notes.b: The trench system made frontal attack costly, and both sides relied on artillery bombardments that often failed to break through.
points: Trenches were defended by barbed wire, machine guns and artillery, and attacks across no man's land exposed attackers to heavy fire.
The German attack on Verdun, from 21 February to 18 December 1916, aimed to bleed the French army white, and it cost both sides several hundred thousand casualties.
The Somme offensive, which began on 1 July 1916, was the largest British attack of the war so far; the first day alone cost the British army about 57,000 casualties, of whom about 19,000 were killed.
The Somme battle ended on 18 November 1916 with Allied gains of only about 10 kilometres at most, at a huge cost in lives.
The Battle of Passchendaele, also called the Third Battle of Ypres, lasted from July to November 1917 and was fought in heavy rain and mud.
Tanks were first used in combat at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916, but they were few in number and mechanically unreliable.
Poison gas was first used on a large scale by Germany at Ypres on 22 April 1915, when chlorine was released against French and Algerian troops.

notes.h: The Eastern Front and Russia's exit
points: The Brusilov Offensive of June 1916 was a Russian attack on the Austro-Hungarian army that gained ground and captured many prisoners, but it could not be sustained.
Russia suffered defeats in 1915 and lost large areas of Poland and the Baltic, and its army suffered shortages of munitions and food.
The Russian Revolution of 1917 led to a new government that made peace with Germany at Brest-Litovsk, which was signed on 3 March 1918.
The Brest-Litovsk settlement gave Germany control over much of Eastern Europe, freeing German divisions for the Western Front in 1918.

notes.h: Other fronts and war at sea
points: The Gallipoli campaign, from the landings of 25 April 1915 to the evacuation of December 1915 and January 1916, failed to open a route to Russia through the Dardanelles.
Italy entered the war on the Allied side in May 1915, but its army suffered a major defeat at Caporetto in October 1917.
The British naval blockade of Germany cut off many imports, while Germany's unrestricted submarine warfare, declared on 1 February 1917, brought the USA into the war.
The Battle of Jutland, on 31 May and 1 June 1916, was the largest naval battle of the war and was indecisive; the German High Seas Fleet returned to port and did not seek a major battle again.

notes.h: Conscription and the mobilisation of manpower
notes.b: The war of attrition required the mass mobilisation of populations, which led states to introduce conscription in the belligerent countries that had relied on volunteers.
points: Britain relied on volunteers until 1916, when the Military Service Act of January 1916 introduced conscription for single men, later extended to married men.
Germany conscripted men from the start of the war, and its Hindenburg Programme of 1916 mobilised industry and labour for total war.
France had conscription in place before 1914, and it mobilised most of its male population of military age.
Conscription led to large casualties among the working class and to tension between governments and trade unions over the use of skilled labour.

notes.h: The entry of the USA and the armistice
points: The Zimmermann Telegram of January 1917, in which Germany proposed an alliance with Mexico against the USA, was published in the American press and increased American anger.
The USA declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917, and American troops arrived in France in large numbers in 1918.
Germany's spring offensive of March 1918, known as the Kaiserschlacht, made large gains but failed to break the Allied line before American reinforcements arrived.
The Hundred Days Offensive, from 8 August 1918 at Amiens, pushed the German army back, and by the end of September the German high command had concluded that the war was lost.
An armistice was signed on 11 November 1918, and fighting ended at 11 a.m. that day.

notes.b: Douglas Haig commanded the British Expeditionary Force from December 1915 to the end of the war, and his strategy at the Somme and Passchendaele was the main focus of later criticism.
points: Douglas Haig was born in Edinburgh in 1861 and had served as a cavalry officer in the Boer War before taking command in France.
He became commander-in-chief of the British Expeditionary Force in December 1915, replacing Sir John French.
He planned the Somme offensive with French forces and continued the attritional battles of 1917, including Passchendaele.
He believed that a breakthrough would come from a sustained attritional campaign and the eventual use of cavalry and combined arms.
He was promoted to field marshal in 1917 and was made an earl after the war.
Contemporaries were divided: King George V and many senior officers trusted him, while Prime Minister David Lloyd George distrusted him and limited his manpower.

Historians differ sharply on his reputation: critics portray him as an unimaginative commander responsible for huge losses, while defenders argue that his strategy was necessary to win the war against the German army.
The phrase lions led by donkeys, often applied to British generals, is a later popular label whose origin is uncertain, and historians have debated it since the 1960s.

notes.h: Assessment: the conduct of the war
notes.b: The war's conduct is judged by whether attrition broke the enemy and at what cost in lives and resources.
points: Achievement: the Allies wore down German manpower in 1916 and 1917, and the German army was exhausted by the time of the 1918 offensives.
Limit: the attritional battles produced huge casualties with little strategic gain, and the Somme and Passchendaele became symbols of waste.
Achievement: the British and French developed tanks, artillery methods and combined-arms tactics that improved the Allied capacity to attack by 1918.
Limit: the Eastern Front collapsed in 1917 and 1918, and the German army in the West held its positions for years despite severe losses.

keyTerms.definition: A war fought across several continents by a large number of states, in which the whole society and economy of each belligerent was mobilised.
A strategy of wearing down the enemy by inflicting heavy losses in men and resources, rather than by a single decisive battle.
The compulsory enlistment of men into the armed forces, which Britain introduced in 1916 and Germany and France had in place from the start.
Fighting from defensive lines of trenches protected by wire and machine guns, which made frontal attacks extremely costly.
The movement of both armies northwards in autumn 1914, which ended with a continuous line of trenches from the North Sea to Switzerland.
The German spring offensive of March 1918, the last major attempt to win the war before American troops arrived in large numbers.

factCards.term: Where and when was the First Battle of the Marne?
factCards.definition: In France, from 5 to 12 September 1914, where the German advance on Paris was checked.

factCards.term: Where did Hindenburg and Ludendorff defeat a Russian army in 1914?
How many casualties did the British suffer on the first day of the Somme?
factCards.definition: About 57,000, of whom about 19,000 were killed.

factCards.term: When did the Battle of Verdun take place?
factCards.definition: From 21 February to 18 December 1916, a German attempt to bleed the French army white.

factCards.term: When did the Battle of Passchendaele take place?
factCards.definition: From July to November 1917, in the Ypres salient and in heavy rain and mud.

factCards.term: Where and when were tanks first used in combat?
factCards.definition: At Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916, during the Somme offensive.
A Russian offensive of June 1916 against the Austro-Hungarian army, which gained ground and took many prisoners.

factCards.term: When was the Military Service Act passed in Britain?
factCards.definition: In January 1916, introducing conscription for single men aged between 18 and 41.
A January 1917 German proposal to Mexico for an alliance against the USA, published in the American press.

factCards.term: When did the USA declare war on Germany?
When did the Hundred Days Offensive begin?
factCards.definition: On 8 August 1918, with an Allied attack at Amiens that pushed the German army back.

factCards.term: When did the armistice take effect?
factCards.definition: On 11 November 1918, when fighting ended at 11 a.m.
